title: Watching Molecules Move by Bleaching a Spot
endLine: Bleach a spot dark; the returning glow measures movement and exchange.

scenes.tts: This glowing membrane looks frozen. How can you see it move? When every protein shines the same green, swapping places leaves the picture unchanged. To reveal motion, you first turn one spot dark.
scenes.caption: This glowing membrane looks frozen. How can you see it move? When every protein shines the same green, swapping places leaves the picture unchanged. To reveal motion, you first turn one spot dark.
scenes.visual: Full-frame top-down schematic microscope view of a cell membrane packed with evenly bright green glowing dots (no molecular structures). The dots subtly trade places in continuous slow ambient motion, yet the uniform green glow looks completely unchanged; a high-contrast question appears ('How can you see it move?'), then a crisp dark circular outline previews one spot in the centre.
scenes.narration: This glowing membrane looks frozen. How can you see it move? When every protein shines the same green, swapping places leaves the picture unchanged. To reveal motion, you first turn one spot dark.

scenes.visual: Over the softly shimmering green membrane world, the title 'Watching Molecules Move by Bleaching a Spot' fades in cleanly in high-contrast text, holds briefly, then fades out while the membrane stays in place.

scenes.tts: First, tag the target molecules with a fluorescent dye or G F P. The tag absorbs blue light and emits green light. A cell making G F P carries its own lamp while alive. Next, a focused laser bleaches one small spot. The molecules stay, but no longer glow.
scenes.caption: First, tag the target molecules with a fluorescent dye or GFP. The tag absorbs blue light and emits green light. A cell making GFP carries its own lamp while alive. Next, a focused laser bleaches one small spot. The molecules stay, but no longer glow.
scenes.visual: Zoom slightly onto the same schematic membrane sheet. Dim grey target dots light up bright green as blue illumination sweeps across and green glow radiates back ('blue in, green out', schematic). A brief bright laser beam focuses onto a circular centre spot; inside that circle, the glowing dots switch to dark charcoal while staying physically present (a small label: 'still there, not glowing'), leaving a sharp dark hole surrounded by bright green dots.
scenes.narration: First, tag the target molecules with a fluorescent dye or GFP. The tag absorbs blue light and emits green light. A cell making GFP carries its own lamp while alive. Next, a focused laser bleaches one small spot. The molecules stay, but no longer glow.

scenes.tts: Then unbleached molecules diffuse sideways into the dark spot as bleached ones wander out. This is fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, or frap. How fast light returns gives the diffusion coefficient, a measure of spreading speed. How completely it returns gives the mobile fraction, the share free to move. Bleaching one spot turns hidden movement into a curve.
scenes.caption: Then unbleached molecules diffuse sideways into the dark spot as bleached ones wander out. This is fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, or FRAP. How fast light returns gives the diffusion coefficient, a measure of spreading speed. How completely it returns gives the mobile fraction, the share free to move. Bleaching one spot turns hidden movement into a curve.
scenes.visual: The glowing membrane shifts smoothly to the left half of the frame while a live schematic plot (labelled 'schematic', axes: spot brightness vs. time) draws on the right. Bright green dots drift sideways into the dark circle while dark bleached dots wander outward. Synchronized with the spot brightening, the curve drops sharply at the bleach mark and climbs smoothly back up. A tangent arrow highlights the steepness ('diffusion coefficient'), and a vertical bracket marks the final height ('mobile fraction').
scenes.narration: Then unbleached molecules diffuse sideways into the dark spot as bleached ones wander out. This is fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, or FRAP. How fast light returns gives the diffusion coefficient, a measure of spreading speed. How completely it returns gives the mobile fraction, the share free to move. Bleaching one spot turns hidden movement into a curve.

scenes.tts: Now watch a second membrane protein after the same laser bleach. The dark spot brightens at first, then stalls at fifty percent of its starting glow. What happened to the other half of those labeled molecules?
scenes.caption: Now watch a second membrane protein after the same laser bleach. The dark spot brightens at first, then stalls at 50% of its starting glow. What happened to the other half of those labeled molecules?
scenes.visual: In the exact same left-membrane, right-curve layout (labelled 'schematic'), the laser flashes again and turns the centre spot dark. Bright green dots begin entering and the curve rises, then flattens cleanly at a dashed 50% line halfway up the starting brightness while the spot stays half-dim. High-contrast question text appears cleanly above the plateau: 'What happened to the other half?'
scenes.narration: Now watch a second membrane protein after the same laser bleach. The dark spot brightens at first, then stalls at 50% of its starting glow. What happened to the other half of those labeled molecules?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. The question remains on screen while the schematic recovery curve pulses gently along the 50% plateau; outside the circle green dots keep drifting freely while inside the circle only half the dots swap.

scenes.tts: Starting from dark, mobile fraction equals recovered brightness divided by starting brightness. Reaching half the starting glow gives fifty percent, so half the labeled molecules cannot move. Often they are anchored to the cytoskeleton.
scenes.caption: Starting from dark, mobile fraction equals recovered brightness divided by starting brightness. Reaching half the starting glow gives 50%, so half the labeled molecules cannot move. Often they are anchored to the cytoskeleton.
scenes.visual: On the right panel, the equation builds piece by piece as spoken: 'mobile fraction = recovered / starting', then 'half / full = 50%'. On the left membrane (schematic), faint underlying cytoskeletal tracks appear beneath the sheet, pinning half of the dark bleached dots firmly inside the bleached circle while the unpinned green and dark dots continue trading places freely.
scenes.narration: Starting from dark, mobile fraction equals recovered brightness divided by starting brightness. Reaching half the starting glow gives 50%, so half the labeled molecules cannot move. Often they are anchored to the cytoskeleton.

scenes.tts: Even full recovery can still mislead you. Frap measures turnover, the swapping of old molecules for new ones. Free diffusion gives turnover, but binding and unbinding at fixed sites give it too. Bleached molecules let go, and glowing ones bind the empty sites.
scenes.caption: Even full recovery can still mislead you. FRAP measures turnover, the swapping of old molecules for new ones. Free diffusion gives turnover, but binding and unbinding at fixed sites give it too. Bleached molecules let go, and glowing ones bind the empty sites.
scenes.visual: The recovery curve on the right rises all the way to full brightness ('schematic'), then the left microscope view smoothly splits into two matching glowing patches that produce the exact same curve: top shows freely diffusing green dots swapping places; bottom shows fixed docking sites where dark bleached dots unbind and drift off while bright green dots bind the empty sites. Label: 'turnover'.
scenes.narration: Even full recovery can still mislead you. FRAP measures turnover, the swapping of old molecules for new ones. Free diffusion gives turnover, but binding and unbinding at fixed sites give it too. Bleached molecules let go, and glowing ones bind the empty sites.

scenes.tts: Some large nuclear bodies may be droplets, a separate liquid phase. Half-body frap tests this. Bleach one half; track both halves and the fluid around them. A droplet has a boundary, so mixing inside should beat crossing its edge. That favours a phase without proving one. Weak edges may slow crossing only a little, and rebinding in clusters mixes internally too.
scenes.caption: Some large nuclear bodies may be droplets, a separate liquid phase. Half-body FRAP tests this. Bleach one half; track both halves and the fluid around them. A droplet has a boundary, so mixing inside should beat crossing its edge. That favours a phase without proving one. Weak edges may slow crossing only a little, and rebinding in clusters mixes internally too.
scenes.visual: The microscope view transitions cleanly into a single large bright green round nuclear body floating in dimmer green nucleoplasm (schematic). The laser bleaches only the left half of the body dark. Bright green dots from the unbleached right half mix across into the bleached left half faster than dimmer dots cross the outer edge, while three simple schematic intensity traces track left half, right half, and nucleoplasm. A subtle dashed boundary softens and internal fixed-site rebinding flickers inside a dense cluster to show why the pattern favours a phase without proving one.
scenes.narration: Some large nuclear bodies may be droplets, a separate liquid phase. Half-body FRAP tests this. Bleach one half; track both halves and the fluid around them. Weak edges may slow crossing only a little, and rebinding in clusters mixes internally too.

scenes.tts: Photobleaching has also tested cell barriers. Textbooks once proposed a sharp forty kilodalton limit for passive passage through nuclear pores. In 2016, Timney and colleagues bleached cytoplasmic fluorescence from different-sized reporters in live budding yeast. Glowing reporters left in the nucleus leaked out through the pores. Their excess signal relaxed toward equilibrium, more slowly for larger reporters, with no sharp cutoff.
scenes.caption: Photobleaching has also tested cell barriers. Textbooks once proposed a sharp 40 kDa limit for passive passage through nuclear pores. Their excess signal relaxed toward equilibrium, more slowly for larger reporters, with no sharp cutoff.
scenes.visual: The same green-fluorescence world pulls back to a schematic live budding yeast cell containing a bright green nucleus and glowing cytoplasm ('Timney et al., 2016'). A sharp vertical '40 kDa?' wall appears briefly and dissolves. The laser bleaches the entire cytoplasm dark, leaving excess green glow inside the nucleus. Glowing reporters of several sizes leak out of the nucleus through the pores: small ones fastest, each larger size a little slower, while paired schematic relaxation curves fall toward equilibrium at graded rates (schematic)—continuous slowing, no sharp wall.
scenes.narration: Photobleaching has also tested cell barriers. Textbooks once proposed a sharp 40 kDa limit for passive passage through nuclear pores. scenes.tts: In 2019, Dawei Yan and colleagues studied plasmodesmata, pores joining plant cells, in an Arabidopsis root mutant. At one interface they saw no pores with a visible cytoplasmic sleeve, the open channel inside. Yet frap showed G F P crossing faster than in wild-type roots. Erasing one patch of light turns hidden exchange into motion you can watch.

scenes.visual: The glowing green view shifts smoothly to two adjacent schematic plant root cells meeting at a cell-wall interface spanned by narrow pores ('Dawei Yan et al., 2019', 'schematic'). On the mutant side, the pores show no open cytoplasmic sleeve; the laser bleaches one cell dark, and green GFP glow streams across the interface into the bleached cell faster than in a smaller wild-type comparison trace beside it. As the dark patch fills back with bright green light, the view widens back into the glowing field.
